captions.instagram:
What is the Doppler effect?

Why does a siren drop in pitch as it passes? Watch each sound wave spread from where the source was, hear the pitch slide as a train goes by, clock a cricket ball with radar, find the wind inside a storm, and push a jet through the sound barrier.

→ Every sound wave spreads from where the siren was, so a moving siren bunches its waves ahead.
→ Bunched waves arrive more often, so you hear a higher pitch. Behind, they stretch and the pitch drops.
→ A passing train’s horn slides down in pitch. It slides, not jumps, because the train does not run through you.
→ Drive past a still horn and it drops too, by a slightly different amount: in air it matters who moves.
→ A radar gun bounces microwaves off a cricket ball. The echo comes back squeezed: Δf = 2 f₀ v ÷ c.

Play with it yourself. It's free and open source: glassbox.how/dopplerclear (link in bio)

youtubeLong.title: What is the Doppler effect? (interactive explainer)
youtubeLong.description:
Why does a siren drop in pitch as it passes? Watch each sound wave spread from where the source was, hear the pitch slide as a train goes by, clock a cricket ball with radar, find the wind inside a storm, and push a jet through the sound barrier.

▶ Play with the interactive version: https://glassbox.how/e/dopplerclear/
⌘ Source code (MIT): https://github.com/bdeeps/dopplerclear

In this video:
• A moving source squeezes its waves. Every crest spreads from where the source was when it made it, at the wave's own speed.
• Why the pitch slides as it passes. A horn at 110 km/h is heard at 439 Hz coming and 367 Hz going.
• An echo is a speedometer. Bounce a wave off something moving and the echo is shifted twice: Δf = 2 f v ÷ c.
• Reading the sky. Weather radar maps the wind inside storms in green and red.
• Where it breaks, and three myths. At Mach 1 the formula divides by zero and the waves pile into a shock cone, heard as a sonic boom all along the flight path.
